The 583 widespread axonal enlargement associated with Aβ deposition might have a significant 584 influence on AD pathology. It has been shown that in the natural animal species, axons 585 with larger diameter have higher transduction speed, for example, in the case of the 586 squid giant axon[33]. However, in the case of AD, the enlarged axons were not natural 587 but instead pathological, which were filled with toxic Aβ, hemorrhagic proteins and 588 destabilized lysosomes. In addition, lysosomal leakage can induce axonal structural 589 damages and increase axolemmal permeability, which might further damage the myelin 590 sheath. Both human and mouse studies indicated that axon diameter increases with 591 aging and cognition decline[34, 35]. There is also a reduced velocity of action potential 592 transmission in AD patients and AD-model transgenic mice[36, 37]. Diffusion tensor 593 imaging studies also indicated that structural damage and disconnection in the white 594 matter is prominent in AD [38, 39]. Axonal amyloidosis and enlargement in AD are 595 likely linked to transduction velocity decrease and white matter damage phenotypes. 596 Besides the basic axonal enlargement phenotype in AD, spheroid formation is also 597 frequently observed. Previous studies showed that spheroid formation on axons also 598 slows down the speed of action potential transduction[40, 41]. JSON: Name: axonal_amyloidosis_pipeline Title: Multiplex immunohistochemistry and quantitative morphometry to determine whether hemorrhage-associated Aβ induces lysosomal destabilization and axonal enlargement in Alzheimer's disease Short Hypothesis: Chronic neuronal uptake of hemorrhage-derived Aβ complexes causes lysosomal destabilization that reduces MAP2 and produces axonal enlargement and spheroid formation. Related Work: Existing work documents extracellular Aβ aggregates and cerebral amyloid angiopathy by histology, reports intraneuronal Aβ accumulation and Aβ-induced lysosomal permeabilization in cell models, and links microhemorrhages to plaque formation. Prior morphometric analyses have characterized dystrophic neurites, phos-Tau-containing neuropil threads, and axonal spheroids, and separate studies have measured lysosomal dysfunction in AD models. Limitations across these approaches include: (1) reliance on single- or few-marker assays rather than multiplexed co-localization across Aβ, lysosomal, cytoskeletal and hemorrhagic markers; (2) sparse quantitative single-lysosome and single-axon morphometry in human tissue; (3) unclear contribution of hemorrhagic proteins (hemoglobin/hemin/ApoE) versus Aβ alone to lysosomal destabilization; (4) limited causal perturbation experiments that block uptake or receptor-mediated entry in physiologically relevant models; and (5) lack of an integrated pipeline bridging human post-mortem tissue, transgenic models, and primary neuron assays. Abstract: We propose an integrated experimental pipeline combining multiplex immunohistochemistry, high-resolution confocal morphometry, and perturbation assays in mouse and primary neuron models to test whether hemorrhage-associated Aβ complexes drive lysosomal destabilization and axonal enlargement in Alzheimer's disease (AD). The pipeline measures single-lysosome size and intensity, axon diameter distributions, MAP2 abundance, phos-Tau, and co-distribution of hemorrhagic markers (HBA, Hemin, ApoE, ColIV, ACTA2) with Aβ. Main contribution: a standardized, quantitative workflow to (1) map co-localization of Aβ and hemorrhagic proteins with lysosomal destabilization at single-cell and single-organelle resolution in human AD tissue, (2) reproduce and manipulate these interactions in APP/PS1 mice and primary neurons, and (3) test uptake and receptor-dependence via endocytosis and sortilin1 perturbation. Expected outcome: a falsifiable mechanistic assignment of hemorrhagic Aβ complexes as drivers of lysosomal failure and axonal pathology, enabling targeted downstream mechanistic studies. Experiments: 1) Human post-mortem cohort: frontal cortex formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded sections from n=20 clinically and neuropathologically confirmed AD donors and n=10 age-matched non-AD controls; 5 non-overlapping 6-8 μm sections per donor. 2) Mouse cohort: APP/PS1 transgenic mice n=10 (12-18 months) and wild-type littermates n=10; perfused, paraffin-embedded frontal cortex, 5 sections/mouse. 3) Primary neuron cultures: rat E18 cortical neurons, N=4 independent culture preparations; treatments (biological replicates each): vehicle, Aβ oligomers (500 nM), hemoglobin (100 μg/mL), hemin (10 μM), Aβ+hemoglobin, Aβ+hemin; exposure durations 24 h, 72 h, 7 d (chronic). 4) Perturbation/ablation arms: sortilin1 siRNA knockdown and dynamin inhibition (dynasore) in cultures; in mice use AAV-shRNA-sortilin1 (n=5) vs scramble (n=5) in APP/PS1 cohort (stereotaxic delivery 6 weeks before harvest). 5) Multiplex markers: Aβ (pan), Cathepsin D, Lamp2, Sortilin1, MAP2, phos-Tau, HBA, Hemin, ApoE, ColIV, ACTA2, nuclear stain. 6) Imaging: confocal z-stacks (60x oil objective) 10 fields per section, 20 sections per donor/mouse total, consistent exposure settings per marker class; electron microscopy of representative regions (n=3 donors, n=3 mice). 7) Measurements: per-axon diameter (perimeter/π and direct line measurement) distribution, % Aβ-positive axons per bundle, spheroid count/mm2, MAP2 mean intensity per soma and per axon, single-lysosome area distribution and Cathepsin D intensity, Pearson and Manders co-localization coefficients, frequency of axon breaks per mm of tract, compound action potential conduction velocity in acute mouse slices (n=6 mice), and cell viability (LDH). 8) Baselines: control human tissue, wild-type mice, vehicle-treated cultures, scrambled shRNA. 9) Comparisons/ablations: (a) human AD vs control; (b) APP/PS1 vs wild-type; (c) culture treatment groups vs vehicle; (d) sortilin1 knockdown/dynamin inhibition vs respective controls to test uptake-dependence; (e) APP/PS1 AAV-shSortilin1 vs APP/PS1 scramble. 10) Statistical analysis: per-metric normality by Shapiro–Wilk, parametric t-test or ANOVA for normal data, Mann–Whitney or Kruskal–Wallis for non-normal; post-hoc pairwise tests with FDR correction; effect sizes reported; power targeted to detect 30% change in mean lysosome size or axon diameter with power=0.8, α=0.05 (sample sizes as above). 11) Ablation/analysis ablation study: quantify reduction in Aβ-lysosome co-localization and lysosome enlargement after sortilin1 perturbation and test downstream MAP2 rescue metrics. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Antibody specificity and cross-reactivity: multiplex panels increase risk of non-specific staining and spectral bleed-through, producing false co-localization. 2) Post-mortem artifacts: variable post-mortem intervals, fixation, and tissue processing may alter lysosomal markers and Aβ detectability and bias effect size estimates. 3) Sampling bias: frontal cortex-focused sampling may not generalize to other regions or AD subtypes. 4) Cross-sectional human data: co-localization is correlational and cannot alone establish causality. 5) Model limitations: APP/PS1 mice and acute cultured neuron exposures may not recapitulate chronic human hemorrhagic Aβ complex exposure and aging-related processes. 6) Perturbation specificity: siRNA/AAV knockdown or pharmacologic uptake inhibitors may have off-target effects that confound interpretation. 7) Quantitative morphometry limits: segmentation errors for small lysosomes or tightly clustered vesicles and manual annotation workload may limit throughput and reproducibility. 8) Statistical and biological variability: inter-donor heterogeneity may require larger cohorts to detect moderate effects. 9) Electrophysiology scalability: ex vivo conduction velocity assays are labor-intensive and limited in sample throughput. 10) Generalization boundaries: findings linking hemorrhagic Aβ complexes to lysosomal destabilization in frontal cortex may not apply to early-stage or non-amyloid AD presentations.
